rv.q: As embodied by these two high-caliber performances, Coble creates a thoughtful, potentially enriching gift to the audience.
Parsons delivers a delightfully nuanced performance with exuberance and sensitivity.

In these moments, and in Ms. Parsons’s more than capable hands, Mr. Coble’s play rises above its slightly formulaic structure to become a dry-eyed, moving rumination on the hard fact that the progress of human life being what it is, truly happy endings are rare indeed.

At 86, Estelle Parsons is almost too sprightly and vigorous to fully convey the indignities of aging in The Velocity of Autumn, Eric Coble’s two-hander play now receiving its Broadway premiere after a previous engagement at Washington, D.C.’s Arena Stage.
Both actors are perfectly fine, but watching them duke it out is only mildly entertaining — the play’s brushstrokes are too broad to paint a compelling portrait.
Even with actors the caliber of Parsons and Spinella, however, this is a once-over-lightly insult to a subject that deserves so much more than a mechanical showcase for gold-standard performers.
Estelle Parsons and Stephen Spinella bring conviction and craft to their roles, but even their considerable skills cannot entirely overcome the play's fundamental flaws.
Ironically, the dominant sensation produced by Eric Coble’s anemic two-hander is also that of growing old.
This new Broadway production is ridiculous not just on the copyright page of the script by Eric Coble but also on every page thereafter.
Both performances are engaging enough to power through what's otherwise well-worn terrain.
It’s a question that hits hard, and one of the many tender moments in the 90-minute play that will rattle you to your core.
Pity the casual theatergoer strolling along 45th Street who spots 'deliciously funny' from down the block and thinks, 'that's for me.'

Eric Coble's 90-minute two-character comedy 'The Velocity of Autumn,' which has arrived on Broadway as a star vehicle for 86-year-old Oscar winner Estelle Parsons and two-time Tony winner Stephen Spinella, is the sort of well-meaning but static and underwhelming play that would be better suited for a budget-conscious regional theater...
But this play elicits a definite response: avoid.
The play itself, however, feels over written.
Too bad their vehicle is so rickety.
